source.title: What Language Model to Train if You Have One Million GPU Hours?
source.authors: Teven Le Scao; Thomas Wang; Daniel Hesslow; Lucile Saulnier; Stas Bekman; Saiful Bari; Stella Biderman; Hady ElSahar; Niklas Muennighoff; Jason Phang; Ofir Press; Colin A. Raffel; Victor Sanh; Sheng Shen; Lintang Sutawika; Jaesung Tae; Zheng-Xin Yong; Julien Launay; Iz Beltagy

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out validation loss across model scales and fits loss against compute, using a scaling-law measurement comparable to the original work, including an English-only fit and multilingual language-specific fits.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own English-only scaling fit and multilingual per-language fits. The architecture ablations, zero-shot benchmark comparisons, and the proposed BLOOM compute allocation are not rows for loss scaling; the allocation relies on a fit rather than testing the optimal parameter/token split. Claims from Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study fits held-out LM loss against compute for its own runs. Figure 1 covers an English-only sweep (125M–13B, about 1e-2 to 1e2 PF-days) with αC≈0.046. Table 9 gives per-language fits L(C)=Cm·C^-αc for a 0.3B–6.0B multilingual sweep. This is the original kind of measurement (power law in compute), so it bears on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with additions. The authors say the English-only fit reproduces Kaplan et al. because the Hoffmann LR schedule was not used. They used it to set an upper bound of 392B params and a minimum of 165B tokens, and chose 176B params at 300–400B tokens. They say scaling coefficients are consistent across well-represented languages, differing in offsets. Small models struggle with underrepresented languages, which larger models handle smoothly.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits held-out loss against compute, but its multilingual fits are per language and use a 0.3B–6.0B model sweep; the English-only allocation fit is described as not accounting for the learning-rate schedule discussed by Hoffmann et al.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports language-dependent fit coefficients and notes end-of-training loss rises for smaller models on Malayalam, Odia, and Telugu. It also says the English-only allocation differs from Hoffmann et al.'s recommendation because the fit did not account for their learning-rate-schedule consideration.
record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The scaling curves in Figure 3 are plotted rather than tabulated by model size, and the text does not report uncertainty for the fit coefficients. The paper describes losses rising at the end of training for three languages among sub-1-billion-parameter models. The English-only fit does not account for the learning-rate schedule discussed in Hoffmann et al.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 3's individual per-model loss points are not separately tabulated; the per-language fitted coefficients from Table 9 and the explicitly described non-smooth language cases are retained instead. No separate row is made for the compute-optimal allocation because the study uses a fitted law to choose an allocation rather than testing parameter/token splits at fixed compute.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters or tokens with the other factor non-bottlenecked. Only loss-vs-compute fits are reported.
All of it. The 13B run is inside the Figure 1 fit, and no held-out larger run is predicted.
All of it. The fit is used to derive an allocation (392B params, 165B tokens), but no splits at fixed compute are swept.
All of it. Shape is chosen from cited work (Kaplan, Levine) and throughput, not from measured loss.
All of it. Only text LM pretraining (multilingual and code) is studied; no other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
All of it. Downstream zero-shot accuracy is reported for ablations, but not as a function of scale or loss beyond a single 1.3B vs 13B pair.
All of it. The Kaplan-vs-Hoffmann gap is attributed to the LR schedule without testing. Per-language exponents (0.030–0.069, no uncertainty) are not analysed as setup-dependence.

missing.what: The largest model (6.0B) loss decreases smoothly for every language. This contrasts with the sub-1B rises and is not recorded as its own row.
missing.locator: Section 5, Language-specific scaling laws paragraph; Figure 3

missing.what: The Figure 1 fit constant (3.01·C^-0.046) and the compute range (~1e-2 to 1e2 PF-days) are absent from the row value.

record.verdict_notes: The record over-linked the language rows to V5 and V7. Multilingual text pretraining is not a different modality or training regime. The study measures no setup or fitting-choice dependence of exponents, and the Hoffmann comparison is discussion only. The per-language fits report no uncertainty, and the end-of-training rises are within-run loss curves, not necessarily the Pareto frontier. Tranche T1 fits the English-only fit; the multilingual fits are a T3-like setting extension within V1.

versions.untested_parts: The reported fits are against compute; the study does not separately establish power laws in parameter count and tokens while holding the other factors non-bottlenecked.
No reported test fits on smaller runs and checks predictions against much larger runs.
The study uses scaling laws to estimate an allocation but does not sweep parameter/token splits at fixed compute to test the loss-minimising allocation.
Model-shape findings are cited, not measured for loss in this study.
The study tests multilingual text pretraining across languages, not other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study reports downstream benchmark results but does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.

The study discusses the learning-rate-schedule difference behind its Kaplan-style allocation and Hoffmann et al.'s alternative; it does not systematically vary fitting methods, parameter counting, or schedules itself.

relationships.condition: English-only sweep 125M–13B, and per-language fits on the 0.3B–6.0B multilingual sweep
relationships.reason: Smooth power-law loss vs compute over about 4 orders of magnitude: αC≈0.046 for English-only (english_compute_fit), and per-language αc of 0.030–0.069 in Table 9.
relationships.display_finding: Loss followed smooth compute power laws with exponent approximately 0.046 for English-only training and 0.030–0.069 across multilingual evaluations.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: English-only sweep 125M–13B, and per-language fits on the 0.3B–6.0B multilingual sweep
source_check.reason: english_compute_fit reports αC approximately 0.046; Table 9 reports per-language exponents 0.030–0.069. Figure 3 fits the best-loss compute frontier.

relationships.condition: Sub-1B models on very underrepresented languages (Malayalam, Odia, Telugu) in a multilingual mix
relationships.reason: Authors report loss rising at the end of training for sub-1B models, so the curves are not monotone declines. The largest model declines smoothly (lang_malayalam, lang_odia, lang_telugu).
relationships.display_finding: Loss rose late in training for sub-1B models on Malayalam, Odia and Telugu, whereas the largest model improved smoothly.
